lessons.title: What is the commissioning compass?
lessons.html:
The compass is:

  • A system assessment tool for change
  • A framework to hold in mind – not a maturity model 
  • Helps you see where change is possible 
  • Reveals what holds your system back 
  • Helps identify your best leverage points for change


What do we mean by system?

When you are commissioning for outcomes, you are connected to a large network of stakeholders, including citizens, communities, organisations, partners and providers. All of this interconnecting network is your system. It makes up the complex whole. 

We have learned from practice in real places.

  • We engaged 60 practitioners in collaboration with the Local Government Association.​
  • We have formally tested in three councils – whole council, adult social care, children's services. ​
  • We have developed the PSTA's Commissioning Academies around the framework of the aspects of the Compass.



What does the compass do?

The goal - helping you navigate complexity and impact on outcomes for people and place

We help you to assess your system and give you a sense of direction about how you can plan to improve.  

The commissioning compass enables you to take a strategic view of commissioning. It lifts you out of just considering the commissioning process (although we cover that too), encouraging you to ask yourself deep, reflective questions, and exploring your context. It helps you see and understand where the pushes and pulls are and identify strengths and areas for improvement. 

You can use the compass just for yourself. Or as a tool for development with your team, across your department or organisation.  

It works best with partners as part of a development process, enabling you to really stretch up into whole system working for wellbeing.  

At the heart of this assessment is how you, as a strategic commissioner, work with complexity. 


Putting the compass into practice

To use the system assessment, first, you assess your system using our 'eight aspects' of commissioning model. These aspects help you to:

  • Appreciate how commissioning works now​
  • Identify where you can focus to unlock change​
  • See the full picture – not a single model​ or perspective 
  • Begin (or continue) a developmental journey

Once you understand your system, use your current position, constraints, and enablers to create an action plan and to select the correct 'commissioning approach'.

Only go into as much detail as you have time for, and as is useful!

lessons.title: Who are we? The PSTA and our offers
lessons.html:
This project was designed and developed by the Public Service Transformation Academy for Care and Health Improvement Programme (CHIP), now referred to as Partners in Care and Health (PCH), which is jointly run by the Local Government Association and Association of Directors of Adult Social Services (ADASS). 

It was produced by RedQuadrant and the Public Service Transformation Academy.

The Public Service Transformation Academy

The Public Service Transformation Academy is a not-for-profit social enterprise, with RedQuadrant as the lead partner. We were founded in 2016 to take over the Cabinet Office's 'Commissioning Academy' programme. Today, we deliver training, consultancy and transformation.

Our mission is to drive better outcomes for people and communities by developing the local, civil, social and health sectors’ capabilities to collaborate, innovate and lead.

The founders of this academy share some core beliefs: That most of the problems the public sector and society is dealing with have a significant underlying level of complexity. This complexity differs – it can arise from having to deal with multiple stakeholders, from complex citizen needs, from a need for cultural or behavioural change, or from a complex system of organisations that need to work together. Often, all these sources contribute to the complexity at the same time.

You can catch up on our latest activity, join our courses, and join our newsletter by following this link: https://link.redquadrant.com/m/PSTAOffers

Commissioning Academy

Set up as a flagship development programme by the Cabinet Office, this unique programme is focused on developing your skills and experience as a commissioner.​It brings together commissioners from across the system – often police, local government, adult social care, children's services, national bodies and many more. ​

We don't focus on rote learning or memorisation – you learn through doing in our action learning approach. Apply your learning to real challenges from your system in a hundred day plan to drive real change.​

lessons.title: Introducing the eight aspects of commissioning
lessons.html:
The system assessment is structured around the eight aspects of commissioning model

The system assessment is structured around the eight 'aspects' of commissioning. An aspect is a part or feature of the total complexity of strategic commissioning. Each aspect looks through a different lens, capturing a wider perspective than traditionally captured in commissioning cycles or definitions. 

Four of the aspects are focused on systems and outcome-based:​

Aspect 1 Whole system design: Work as one place to support and enable wellbeing, sustainability and mutual support.

  • Key question: Are we making a place that helps everyone live life well?​

Aspect 2 Relationships and organisation across the system: Everyone focused on achieving shared goals with aligned incentives and funding 

  • Key question: Is everyone working together coherently across our place?​

Aspect 3 Capacity, capability, and confidence: Shape markets, provision, and delivery of all those (place, assets, VCFSE, employees, families, friends, carers, neighbours, community, etc) who enable people can live their lives well

  • Key question: Are we building the ability to meet or prevent needs, across all sectors?​

Aspect 4 Citizen, place, and outcome centred: Citizens in charge of their own outcomes, with success measured by people’s views on whether and to what extent they can live their lives well 

  • Key question: Is the work led by the people or place who need it, and measured according to the outcomes they get?​


The other four are the foundational pillars of commissioning: ​

Aspect 5 Information, insight, and innovation: Commissioning that focuses on innovation and creativity and based on robust information / insight

  • Key question: Is the work led by the people or place who need it, and measured according to the outcomes they get?​

Aspect 6 Making room to make a difference: Meeting, interpreting, and actively shaping the policy and legal requirements that we have to work within

  • Key question: Do we understand and shape the law and policy we are working with? ​

Aspect 7 Commissioning process: Technically excellent, clear, and robust arrangements

  • Key question: Do we have a strong, effective process?​

Aspect 8 Models and tactics: Design of delivery and intervention models that are fit for purpose, effective, and innovative, based on real attention to how intervention and infrastructure are structured and delivered

  • Key question - Do we understand what makes a difference on the ground?

lessons.title: Instructions for the system assessment
lessons.html:
There are six steps to carrying out the full exercise:

You can go into as much or as little detail as you wish with this assessment.  

If you want to have a strategic overview you can just complete steps one and two.

For a more analytical view, also do step three.

For the assessment to inform an action or development plan you will need to additionally complete step four and five.

And for the super advanced level, step six is for you! 


Step One -Getting started

Spend a bit of time familiarising yourself with the 'eight aspects of commissioning.

Understand how the top four are outcomes-focused, and systems-based and the bottom four are the foundational pillars. 

Aspect 1, Whole system design: Work as one place to support and enable wellbeing, sustainability and mutual support.

Aspect 2, Relationships and organisation across the system: Everyone focused on achieving shared goals with aligned incentives and funding 

Aspect 3, Capacity, capability, and confidence: Shape markets, provision, and delivery of all those (place, assets, VCFSE, employees, families, friends, carers, neighbours, community, etc) who enable people can live their lives well

Aspect 4, Citizen, place, and outcome centred: Citizens in charge of their own outcomes, with success measured by people’s views on whether and to what extent they can live their lives well 

The other four are foundational pillars: ​

Aspect 5, Information, insight, and innovation: Commissioning that focuses on innovation and creativity and based on robust information / insight

Aspect 6, Making room to make a difference: Meeting, interpreting, and actively shaping the policy and legal requirements that we have to work within

Aspect 7, Commissioning process: Technically excellent, clear, and robust arrangements

Aspect 8, Models and tactics: Design of delivery and intervention models that are fit for purpose, effective, and innovative, based on real attention to how intervention and infrastructure is structured and delivered


You need to have solid scores on the foundational pillar 'aspects' to be able to effectively move to be aspirational in the top four 'aspects'

Give your place an instinctive score on how you are doing in terms of each of the 'eight aspects'. Do this quickly. It is just your first pass, your gut reaction. 

We will encourage you to revisit this after working through the questions for the aspects. 

Scores are categorised as below. Note that scores of 70 and above have been rare in system-assessments so far. ​

  • 0 – 24 Poor (significant risk)​
  • 25 – 49 Fair (lesser/lower risk, improvement required) ​
  • 50 – 74 Good (opportunities identified/issues need to be addressed) ​
  • 75 – 100 Excellent (no action required)​


Step Two - self-assessment questions

You will have already recorded a score for each of the eight aspects, based on your initial gut feeling. ​

Next, work through the assessment questions. These are encouraging you to take a deeper look at your system and develop more curiosity. Score your 'system' on each question.  

If you are doing this as a team and each person scored individually, do not simply average your results – look at the overall pattern of highs and lows, open up the conversation about what people are seeing in the system to give that score.​

In a workshop, this can be a great way to use appreciative or action enquiry. It will help you to be curious about how stakeholders experience each aspect and what the knock-on impact of that is. This will help too with the next step. 

At the end, we’ll compare your initial gut reactions to your actual score.​ Again, we ask you to be curious about where there are differences or alignment. What is that telling you? 

If you want to have a more deeply analytical view now move onto step three. If you want a lighter, quicker dive into your commissioning, skip step three and head on to step five.


Step Three - Factors that constrain and enable

For each aspect, you are provided with a list of 'factors in place that constrain and enable'. These are important influences on your commissioning, some of which may be blockers (constraints) and others of which may provide opportunities or advantages (enablers). Which hold you/ the system back? Which supports you most to achieve change and outcomes? ​

Be curious about the depth of your awareness or understanding of each of the factors. You may wish to explore the factors further before you score them, but this is not essential at this stage. You can pick that up in your action plan later.  

Once you have discussed each of the factors that constrain and enable, select the three most important enablers and the three most important constraints for each of the eight aspects. 

If undertaking this assessment with stakeholders, it is likely that there will be very different perspectives in the system. In your workshops, think about how you can explore these perspectives to give you a deeper understanding of your system relationships. There are not right and wrong answers here. This is to provide you with insight and intelligence to identify where to intervene for the most effective change.  


If you want to develop this assessment into an action plan or commissioning development plan, we recommend you complete steps four and five. Use your assessment to determine the possible commissioning approaches.

The action plan needs to include all of the insights and actions you have captured along the way in your exploration, curiosity and conversations.


Step Four - Control and influence. Urgent and important 

Once you have evaluated the most enabling and constraining factors for each aspect, you can move to determine what is in your control and what do you need to influence.  

Whether the factor is:  

  • in your control  
  • influenceable 
  • out of your control 

whether, in the opinion of the group, the factor is:  

  • to be boosted  
  • not to be boosted 
  • would benefit from innovation or experimentation 

You can arrive at this by exploring the following questions. 

  • How will we boost the enabling factors in our control?
  • How can we influence partners and stakeholders about enabling factors out of your control?
  • For constraining factors within our control, what actions can we take to overcome them? 
  • How will we use our influence where we can, to reduce constraining factors and build on enabling factors? 
  • How will we take account of and work around constraining factors that are not in our control? 
  • What experiments can we run to look at constraining factors that require innovation? 
  • Which of these are the most urgent? 
  • Which of these are the most important? 
  • Which of these would require the most work? 
  • Are there any “quick wins”? 

We suggest you use an action plan to capture your actions here. If desired, this action-planning can be developed into a Commissioning Development Plan. 

Action planning on the factors that constrain or enable can help you to expand your ‘elbow room’ - your space and power to make an impact on effective commissioning. 

Doing this activity across all eight of the aspects at once is quite a big task. We suggest you take the bottom four aspects first giving you twenty-four constraints and enablers to work from. Develop an overall plan for these. When looking at the top four, you may need a separate plan for each.  


Step Five - Exploring approaches to commissioning

As you can see from the assessment, we are opening up all of the different ways to assess your strategic commissioning system. The aspects help you see 'what' the system contains and here we introduce the 'approaches’ to commissioning, which help you assess 'how' to intervene.  

You can approach commissioning in different ways, with different methods, different principles, and different means. We have classified this through our eight 'approaches' to commissioning. Here is a summary of those approaches.  

Approach 1, Place-based wellbeing: Design and creation of a place-based wellbeing system.

Approach 2, Leadership of place for whole system change: Creating a system that works.

Approach 3, Unlocking potential: A place where everyone can thrive. 

Approach 4, Citizen-centred commissioning: empowering citizens within the system.

Approach 5, Values-based/disruptive commissioning: Changing the status quo

Approach 6, Strategic procurement of services against needs: Services that meet demand 

Approach 7, Market management: Creating conditions for best value and outcomes within financial constraints.

Approach 8, Delivery model design: Effective delivery models enabling effective practice.

You can find more details for each of the 'approaches' on the pages for each of the 'aspects' of commissioning here on teachable. This will allow you to explore in more detail all the options available to you and your system.  


Step Six – Not for the faint-hearted!

Now if you are the person at school who always wanted the stretch questions, the advanced level....here is one for you in this assessment.

Once you understand your score on the eight aspects of commissioning, you can use this to select your most appropriate approach to commissioning. 

Return now to your scoring for the eight aspects that you did at the beginning. Add those scores into the table here. 

Then read down the table from the top to the bottom 

The first score over 50, reading down the table, identifies the recommended strategic commissioning approach.  

But critically, it must not have a lower score beneath it in the table.

For example:

Aspect Score (/100) Approach Focus
1. Whole system design 20 Place-based wellbeing
2. Relationships and organisation across the system 60 Leadership of place for whole system change Aspirational focus area with substantial risk. Substantial action to reinforce below otherwise system vulnerable to shock if key partners leave.
3. Capacity, capability and confidence 30 Unlocking potential
4. Citizen, place, and outcome centred 20 Citizen-centred commissioning
5. Information, insight and innovation 60 Values-based/disruptive commissioning Aspirational focus area with risk reinforce below
6. Making room to make a difference 40 Strategic procurement of services against needs Strengthen
7. Commissioning process 60 Market management Primary focus area
8. Models and tactics 55 Delivery model design Maintain and improve

In this example, the system has been given a mix of scores and you could interpret it several ways.

You might be tempted to focus on approach 2, 'Leadership of the place for whole system change', because it is high up on the table and you have a high score. We would suggest that you don't, because some of the lower down aspects – the ones that are foundational – have weaker scores of below 50. This example is particularly weak in aspect 4 ('citizen, place, and outcome centred' and also has weaknesses in aspects 3 and 6 ('Capacity, capability, and confidence' and 'Making room to make a difference'). 

In the example, we would suggest that you focus on fixing the foundations which involves focusing on some of the aspects lower down in the table. If you want to pick a single commissioning approach then in this example you would benefit from 'Market management'. If you instead opt for a blend of approaches then consider researching 'market management' and 'Delivery model design', which are both within your grasp and 'strategic procurement of services against needs', and 'values-based/disruptive commissioning', which are both a bit more advanced than your current practice.

The assessment of your system will help you understand why you have these undermining features and whether there are quick wins to resolve them, allowing you to move up the approaches for more impact. 

Note that scores of over 70 are very unusual. If you do not score over 50 in any aspect, then you will need to begin with the foundational aspect of 8. Models and Tactics. 

In summary, an approach higher in the table, is only sustainable if the commissioning aspects lower down the table can support it. They are the foundations. If the lower aspects are not achieving a high score the risks are higher. It is not impossible to apply a higher approach. But you need to do it with the awareness that your basics and foundational practice needs boosting, scaffolding or nurturing in the process. 

Considering the approaches in this way allows you to critically appraise, or to opt for a blend of approaches, sense-checking your understanding of your challenges, bringing in your insights on your constraints and enablers and any associated action-planning you have developed. A blend of approaches may be useful at different times and in different commissioning situations.

lessons.html:
You can approach commissioning in different ways: with different methods, different principles, and different means. We have classified this through our 'eight approaches to commissioning model:

Approach 3, Unlocking potential: A place where everyone can thrive. 

Approach 4, Citizen-centred commissioning: empowering citizens within the system.

Approach 5, Values-based/disruptive commissioning: Changing the status quo

Approach 6, Strategic procurement of services against needs: Services that meet demand 

Approach 7, Market management: Creating conditions for best value and outcomes within financial constraints.

Approach 8, Delivery model design: Effective delivery models enabling effective practice.

Once you understand your score on the eight aspects of commissioning, you can use this to select your most appropriate approach to commissioning.

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

Our place has a highly integrated health and care system, with shared organisational leadership. We have mapped out need across the area and have a simple system of identifying five levels of need. Most of our work is structured around localities, which are engaged with the community, voluntary, and faith sectors, partly thanks to our very ambitious investment programme in that space. We have not quite got the balance of in-house and contracted provision right yet, as we still have some fairly inflexible whole-place provider contracts and some are struggling, but we are planning to bundle this differently the next time we procure, to connect better to localities.

We are experimenting in a few localities with self-organising social care and district nursing teams, and in one with dementia-friendly places. In others, where there are problems with the night-time economy, mental health, and hospital admissions, on working closely with the police, particularly at ‘hot spot’ times, we also have a key-worker service for people with very high levels of ambulance and A&E utilisation.

Ward councillors, advice services, and community groups play a role in steering locality decisions and signposting need. We are starting to engage deeply with carers and service users and have plans to bring them in to locality governance. As we had identified mental health issues and physical health as priority areas for intervention and prevention, we are working on locality-based strategies for green spaces and fitness offers, as well as seeking innovative ideas around counselling services.

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We are trying to join up locally through sharing data and planning, but outside of the formal governance structures, this does not fully carry through. There was a legal dispute between the council and clinical commissioning group about continuing healthcare funding several years ago, which resulted in some historic “bad blood” and a lack of trust. The data, at least, is useful, though we do not think it is completely accurate, as we are a ‘green and leafy’ place where we see an outflow of younger families and professionals and an inflow of retirees. Though the retirees are often relatively wealthy, increased costs of living can really bite.

We are struggling with high demand for vulnerable adult services including dementia, so that is taking up a lot of our time and attention and we are seeking more funding and to create early intervention and prevention services. We are not getting much of a response from the market on innovation and new opportunities and increased funding, even though they complained when we did a care cost and quality exercise that our focus on driving down costs was holding them back from offering us new ideas and options.

We have worked with housing associations to handle access to our limited residential care but are worried about the implications of future Care Act changes. We are beginning the journey of multi-disciplinary teams in a few locations, but there is real concern about how it will impact on social worker caseloads and time with clients, particularly as some of our clients are relatively isolated and travel times are lengthy. A major concern is the increasing number of residential care planning applications being approved, which will inevitably increase our demands and costs.

﻿Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

Whole system design is likely to highlight issues of inequality and inequity in conditions and access to services. Care should be taken to include marginalised voices in governance, leadership, and delivery, and to resist picking ‘quick wins’ which may further exclude marginalised and under-served groups.

The first aspect of commissioning, Whole system design, is closely connected with the first approach to commissioning, Place-based wellbeing.

lessons.title: Definition: Relationships and organisation across the system
Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

Our relationships have taken a lot of work to get where they are today. We had a legacy among lead members and senior NHS executives of some highly volatile and difficult individuals, failed attempts to engage with and form a coalition of the voluntary and community sector, tough provider negotiations, and a tradition of commissioners who were very good technically and delivered mostly good processes, but didn’t engage much with individuals outside of the formal processes. There was a feeling that everyone was trying to pass on costs to everyone else, and trust was low.

Things started to change with a new political leadership which coincided with several senior leaders moving on. This offered an opportunity to address and reset some of the resentments that still simmered. We started to build a new outcomes-focused plan as we entered into ICS planning and held a facilitated session which encouraged us – in a safe way – to air all those old opinions about each other. Although that was not comfortable, we found it was safe, and important, to do, and set a new tone.

The real breakthrough was joint locality visits – we went jointly (social care, health, and political leaders) to engage with staff and citizens in various places, and to hear people’s experience of our care system first-hand. That was very powerful and led to things like people with experience on our decision-making boards and regular back-to-the floor and mystery shopping exercises which have helped to keep us all focused on the big picture. That does not mean there have not been some really strong disagreements, but those have more often been useful than destructive. We are really focused on broadening beyond the ICS plans to include coproduction, providers, community groups, and other parts of the council and public services who can help.

We eventually learned that all the credit we gained with providers with really good up-front engagement was lost with a very stiff and formal procurement process – which presented providers with a fait accompli after all our talk of partnering and coproduction – and then weak contract management, even when they were coming to us with innovative ideas. We are working on that now, and that involves building a much better partnership with procurement and commercial colleagues.

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We thought our relationships were good, but now I don’t think that’s true. We have a place-based plan, part of our local strategic partnership, which is based on place-based data, but while everyone comes to the partnership board meetings, we have realised that agreement in that meeting does not mean that partner services change in line with this and that people working on the ground do not know about the plan at all. 

A recent resident door-knocking exercise (following on from our experience during Covid) suggested that our understanding of vulnerability and care needs in our strategic documents might not be that accurate. We created a provider forum, but that got bogged down in price discussions and attendance is really low now. We also tried to do community engagement with ward-based ‘town hall’ meetings but they became a miserable experience that officers try to get out of attending, dealing with complaints and negativity.

We have realised now that we do need to do something about this, and that commissioners are quite well-placed to have an influence, so we are working to connect – through listening to suppliers, citizen groups and frontline care workers, at first. And the Mayor has set up informal networking before the strategic partnering meetings. We know there is a lot of work to do on this! 


Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

Good quality relationships allow the challenging of issues to be done safely.  They need to be built for the long-term and embedded, for inequality to be challenged and overcome. Relationship-building must consciously include formerly-excluded groups, if it is to be valuable.  Commissioners and systems need to be aware of the risk that a focus on building relationships can reduce the willingness to challenge norms and problematic issues.

A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

Unlocking potential is the heart of our strategic commissioning approach. We have invested significantly in community development, shifted several large contracts over time from large commercial national providers to small local providers (leading to more money recycled in the local economy, more quickly, making a real impact on people on the edge of poverty). Adult wellness – building from our Ageing Better programme – is a core service and part of a joined-up, place-based strategy (mostly led by the council, but we’re working on it!) which links with lifelong learning, town centre generation, and access to good work to try to deal with poverty, low skills, and low productivity largely due to ill health. Our community connection activities are also linked to social prescribing and remuneration for co-production work, governance roles, and consultation. 

We now routinely commission with a mix of grants, contracts, and mixed models, offering long-term funding where possible, covering overheads, seeking minimal or no bid costs where possible (this has proved much harder to do for NHS spend given the regulations). Alliance contracting has proved helpful for this. Where we do traditional contracting, we have strong social value commitments – and, more importantly, contractual commitments – to social outcomes, co-production, quality of employment, and joining our provider collaborative to look at workforce development (and recruitment and retention) as a whole place. We also have a commitment to map existing assets and delivery servicing before bringing in new contracts, and to have a market development plan which shows how each contract will leave our provider markets healthier.

All of this has been really difficult, and we could not have achieved it without staunch support from senior leaders and politicians, and without linking to their priorities for the council and place as a whole. It helped to have money to invest. Many commercial providers have also been very positive, particularly about freedom to innovate during service delivery.

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We have had to cut our grants to the voluntary sector and use social prescribing and asset-based approaches as ways of mitigating service savings, as funding has reduced and thresholds for access have increased. We are currently reviewing our information, advice, and guidance contract and hope to make cuts and award to a single provider (with sub-contractors) to be able to manage the relationship better and demonstrate better value for money. We have introduced standard social value clauses and a requirement for local investment and a proportion of local sub-contracting. We commission a lot of capability building and support services, but usually small scale and not joined up.

Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

It is important to take a critical perspective regarding the impact of deprivation, exclusion, and intersectional factors on the capability of people to provide their own support, and not make assumptions about this capability. Additionally, some people who are otherwise in highly privileged groups will not necessarily be privileged (in terms, for example, of close and engaged social networks) when it comes to their ability to be supported in their home and community. At the same time, traditional service provision is likely to be biased and have built-in assumptions about needs and how they should be met, which will impact different groups in different ways. The same suspension of assumption and genuine exploration needs to apply to groups and organisations providing support, which may have very different perspectives, strengths, and weaknesses depending on their context.

lessons.title: Definition: citizen, place, and outcome centred
Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

We work hard to base all service provision on “what do you really need?” conversations with citizens. We give social workers and others who have these conversations a lot of discretion to meet needs directly, based on these conversations (within budgetary limits), and pilots show that this reduces the overall cost of care. We have expanded this to an advocacy/case management role when appropriate. A few years ago, we mapped out entire user journeys and found that our own systems being unable to hear what people were actually asking for was costing us millions in incorrect specifications with serious knock-on effects. It has been a long journey to build everyone’s trust in a focus on understanding and meeting needs opposed to formal assessment processes, and we are going through another version of that journey now as we introduce more community options and social prescribing. We have some senior politicians on board and a new DASS who is really supportive. A breakthrough moment came when we took the finance director on a site visit, and they saw that we were working on real value not on budgets – but that it was also good for budgets. 

To be honest, our approach has probably slowed integration and we are still struggling to make it work in the NHS, but we have confidence we will get there. We are linking to the NHS “Getting It Right First Time” (GIRFT) programme, to try to communicate it better. We also now have enthusiastic fans amongst the user base, who are powerful advocates. We still have lots of traditional contracts and formally assessed provision – but at minimum we are including user feedback (“did you get what you needed?” and so on) as part of the evaluation criteria and building in learning and adaptation – our big lesson has been that learning is key.

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We attempted once to create a marketplace for self-funders from which we would also call off services, and a combination of technological and market challenges and leadership challenges meant that it was seen as a failure, so there is a real fear of being too ambitious in this space. We are working hard on social care and health integration and hearing a lot about avoiding ‘unwarranted variations’ in provision.  

We are really pushing to move to what are called ‘outcomes-based contracts’ – in fact, our providers are leading us to some extent on that. But that is usually based on our assumptions and definitions of outcomes. We are aware that access to our services is messy and confusing, and it is hard for people to get what they really want, so we have commissioned two specialist information advice and guidance services (for dementia and carer support) as tests. 

Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

Equality and equity must be central to this aspect, because making assumptions about care outcomes or forcing individuals into standardised processes, services, and systems of care presents perhaps the greatest risk to a fair and equitable system. At the same time, attempts to ‘put citizens in the driving seat’ also risk a bias towards historically privileged groups and meeting or supporting the needs of those who are best able to access decision-makers and communicate in familiar and accepted ways. Therefore, co-production and advocacy must enable appropriate representation and must be done in a way and in a context that guards against these risks.

lessons.title: Definition: Information, insight, and innovation
Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

We’ve tried to play it clever in commissioning, since social care here used to be very traditional and siloed – we have built alliances, supported services in crisis (even when timescales meant we couldn’t really follow the process we would have liked), done mini-training for everyone in the directorate, and even ensured that we win a few awards for innovations, sharing credit with the services. We work closely with the team that used to be our Health and Care Observatory, and with the teams supporting governance at council and ICS level. We also work closely with the Finance Business Partners, who are critical to what gets approved, or not, in the annual budget. 

We have run dedicated external and in-house capability-building, most of it based on action learning and pulling in mixed teams from across different council services and partners to work on real problems and build relationships. We also made co-commissioning with user and citizen voice groups part of our journey from the start, and have affinity groups, citizen commissioners, and we’re about to engage with our first Citizen Jury – this one is on the climate crisis so there’s some important overlaps, but we want to learn the process before running one on learning disabilities and transitions from children’s social care, as both are major issues in our borough.

We have also found that community groups and providers are some of our biggest allies – we recently let a home care contract in a way that both invited innovative bids and encouraged ongoing innovation in service delivery, designed by users and care staff, and we have found even some losing providers have been in touch, keen to share the model elsewhere.

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We have had a few false starts with ‘commissioning’ – on one extreme we went to a whole-council commissioning model, but there was not enough clarity about how that worked, and commissioners and providers reported to the same line managers. There also was not much recognition of how adult social care was different. Then we went to the other extreme and for a while the main team with the ‘commissioner’ job title was the team processing direct payments. We now have a team in social care with the job title ‘strategic commissioner’, but they have to go to services for most of their data, and Members and our partnership boards have expressed the opinion that ‘commissioning is over’ (it’s still associated with the ‘purchaser/provider split’). At the moment, most of their skills are around important technical areas such as the legal requirements for market shaping, but we are planning some development work and actually commissioning plays a big role in our service planning, due to some major contracts coming up where big savings are earmarked.


Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

Without good information, the opportunity to innovate and change, and the skill to do so, the cause of equality and equity cannot be effectively advanced. Care must be taken not to make insights a reflection of our own prejudices.  Engaging excluded voices and welcoming active challenge is one powerful tool to guard against this. It is important to establish and stick to agreed values in this space. The inequality in power dynamics between commissioners and populations becomes starker when commissioners are more powerful and more effective, but effective commissioners can also be the most direct route towards redressing this balance. Empowering communities as commissioners empower themselves is a powerful way to address this paradox.

lessons.title: Key questions
lessons.html:
• Do we really understand all the needs in our place, including the unmet need?
  • Do we have an ambitious and clear adaptive route map for change?
  • Do we practice active learning and insight development?
  • Do we have a culture of innovation, experimentation and learning from failure (and success)?
  • Do we commission from a values-driven position, taking responsibility for outcomes while avoiding the ‘heroic’ mode of ‘fixing everything’ in favour of an enabling approach where people feel involved and part of designing and implementing things that matter to them? And we involve the workforce in design.
  • Are we using approaches that harness complexity and an appreciation of whole systems?
  • Do we work across different paradigms as appropriate, based on multiple perspectives?

Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

We have done lots of work to make sure we really understand what we are doing regarding compliance. We built policies with the legal team, people with lived experience, and excluded groups, and we engaged with health colleagues to make sure we had a consistent approach (and necessary differences were clearly identified). We worked with policy and procurement people to shape ways of working we could reliably keep to, so that, along with all our business cases, we have a compliance case and a fuller equalities impact assessment. 

It is a lot of work but because we have really worked it through, it adds value. It also makes it much harder for people to criticise our work once it has been through the whole process. We became a Social Value case study and we are talking with DHSC about adopting the new white paper guidance early, which gives us the opportunity to feed back (and is going to be quite important for our financial sustainability).

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We do occasionally run into problems with procurement telling us that our most innovative plans are not a good fit with policy, and often that has to go to the corporate management team to get resolved. We have also had a couple of challenges under the Equalities Act which caused us to reconsider some big recommissioning work. 

In general, we understand the framework we have to work within, and we stick to it – this also means that when working with users and practitioners, we have the cover of the Care Act to be able to push through required changes. We had to follow the council policy on social value, which was a bit of a missed opportunity, and our approach to market shaping actually needs to be shaken up a bit – that will be an opportunity to work with providers to come up with something a bit more fit-for-purpose – just in time for the new requirements!


Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

A strong policy and compliance approach to equality is very important, as is responding to compliance requirements with equality and equity in mind. It is important to recognise that compliance with regulation is not a full answer to supporting equality, diversity, and inclusion, but just the beginning.

lessons.title: Definition: commissioning process
Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

Increasingly, all our commissioning is done across partners, with providers and in co-production with people who draw on services. This means that we are putting much greater emphasis on getting a good and legally compliant process in place – but we see that as a platform to work together on ongoing learning and practice. In a recent homecare contract, we were participating in weekly sprint meetings at one stage as service patterns were developed jointly with carers and service users. We were paying close attention to the implications for cost, but it did come in within the budget envelope, and we learned a lot. We have found it useful to blend different sources of data to understand what a service can provide – from service users, practitioners, population data, things we’ve picked up from elsewhere, and so on. Extra Care housing was a major capital investment, so that side of things was a much stricter, more formal process, however we want to go back to prototyping how the service actually works once the buildings are ready to run.

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We follow the classic commissioning process. The challenge is that we never have enough time. When we can do it, we really go to town and thoroughly analyse high-quality data to identify needs, current provision, gaps, opportunities for innovation etc to come up with a ‘perfect spec’. The challenge is that, often, we just get squeezed out of time to do that properly and by the time we go to market we often find we are having to make in-year savings, so a lot of that work can feel insignificant.

Even in less-than ideal contracts with problematic providers, we often end up running the contract for an extra year to give ourselves time to run a proper OJEU process. As part of trying to stretch budget to meet needs, we are increasingly letting very long contracts to try to support lower prices and meet some of the needs of the voluntary and community sector. Because we want to start at the start and get the specification right, and because of all these challenges, we probably are not great on contract management. When we get the time, we do a thorough lessons learned exercise at contract close – part of feeding into the needs specification. Overall, I think we could be closer to practice, and we find co-production hard to get right. We have also found it hard to align our processes with those of partners, who seem to operate in very different ways.


Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

A strong process needs to build in the following elements:

  • Understanding of unmet and marginalised need
  • Access for those who may be excluded
  • Strong equality and equity in specification and contract management
  • Co-design and shared learning with excluded groups

lessons.title: Definition: models and tactics
Case studies and Equality and equity considerations
lessons.html:
A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

We work on service design alongside strategic commissioning and have a system of ‘circles’ which connect selections of practitioners, carers, those with lived experience etc to talk about practice and share and expand on good ideas. These have enabled us to really build on earlier assistive technology work and this is becoming a major feature of some of our work. We have also identified lots of opportunities to improve joining-up and signposting between services, which has saved significant amounts from our advice contract as well as provided much earlier intervention to support citizens who would otherwise have been put off from asking for care until much later.

We have recently merged three smaller contracts, shared one across health and social care, and considered a public sector mutual for a former in-house service (though in the end the employees preferred the TUPE option). We have co-designed a new carer support service which is borough-wide and mostly provided through mutual aid. In general, we find that really understanding delivery model options and how they might affect practice on the ground is a ‘superpower’ when it comes to getting buy-in from social workers and other staff, and from politicians. 

A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

We tend to consider delivery models only at the contractual level, and probably miss some opportunities for innovation. We did recently put out a tender for some innovation work, particularly around new technology, and we are looking forward to seeing how that goes. We recently consolidated our information, advice, and guidance contracts and saved a lot of money along with creating improved referral journeys. We have noticed that second-tier councils and housing providers are a significant part of competition for workers with our care services, so we need to work out how to address that. Most of our work with providers post-contract is monitoring and focusing on cost reduction opportunities and making sure they stick to the service provision agreed in the contract. 

Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

It is with practice on the ground, enabled by delivery models, that equality and equity are either supported or fail. It is important to think about the implications of changes in delivery models, particularly innovative ones and those using novel technology (or with digital access) for those who are traditionally marginalised and excluded, and groups who could be marginalised or excluded by the new model.

  • How to move toward: Engage users, map processes, and learn from service design innovations elsewhere.
  • What to do: Link design with real practice, co-develop models, and ensure practical implementation.
  • What not to do: Avoid rolling out untested models or becoming fixated on structure over impact.
  • Risks and issues: May challenge entrenched interests and stretch delivery capacity if not managed well.
  • Commissioning skills and structure: Needs design thinkers with operational understanding and credibility across services.

lessons.html:
The documents below are final drafts from the earlier version of the 'Commissioning Compass' project. It was formerly known as the 'Strategic Commissioning Options Appraisal' and then renamed 'Applying a strengths-based methodology to your strategic commissioning'. The versions produced for the LGA had a specific focus on adult social care.
